title: Bound To Earth, But Still Flapping Its Wings Hard

contact_edits.before: In fact, there is some Canadian content here. John Jarvis plays, deliriously well, a fellow who goes humorously mad and starts speaking with a Canadian accent. I'm not suggesting these conditions are coequal; his character is a traumatised war vet who starts channelling a slain Newfie comrade. He even talks of moving to Canada, though neither he nor the play gets far in this direction. He also has apocalyptic visions in which he foresees the atomic bomb, the oil race and Monty Python. Others delightful are Paul Braunstein as a dogged but not quite dashing seducer, and as the oracular aunt, the still-youngish Michelle Fisk taking subtle advantage of age's privilege to stay comparatively still and quiet. Julie Stewart puts on a bold comic face as a semi-willing adulteress (the spirit is willing, etc.) and John Cleland blusters effectively as the bathroom magnate. Of the two putative heroines, Lisa Norton has an intriguingly baleful air as Martha the reluctant, not to say incompetent, maid; Kerry Ann Doherty smiles prettily as Jane, but the character's a hole in the play. As a text, And Up They Flew is earthbound, but the production flaps wings. - And Up They Flew runs until April 4 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit theatrecolumbus.ca.
